newsitem.title: CANADA: Avenor offers to buy troubled Repap Enterprises.
newsitem.headline: Avenor offers to buy troubled Repap Enterprises.

text.p: Avenor Inc. proposed Wednesday to buy troubled pulp and coated paper company Repap Enterprises Inc. in a C$3.3 billion ($2.4 billion) transaction that would create Canada's second-largest forest products company.

Avenor said it was making an all-stock offer of one newly issued Avenor share for 4.25 shares of Repap, a transaction valued at C$617 million ($457 million). Including Repap's roughly C$2.6 billion ($1.85 billion) of debt and convertible debentures, the total value of the takeover is C$3.3 billion ($2.4 billion), Avenor officials said.

The transaction, expected to close Feb. 28, would give the combined company C$5 billion ($3.7 billion) of annual sales, making Montreal-based Avenor Canada's second-largest forest products company after MacMillan Bloedel Ltd., of Vancouver.
It would also leave Avenor with more than C$3.2 billion ($2.4 billion) of debt and bank credit lines, pushing its debt-to-equity ratio to 59:41.

Shares of both Avenor and Repap, which is also based in Montreal, tumbled on news of the offer. Avenor shares slipped $C2.50 on the Toronto Stock Exchange to C$18.70 before recovering to C$19.25. Shares of Repap were down $C1.10 to $C4.40.

In a telephone conference with reporters, Avenor Chairman and Chief Executive Paul Gagne said the Repap purchase would expand Avenor's product lines beyond pulp and newsprint to higher value-added products such as coated paper, which is mainly used in magazines.
"We wanted to move up the value chain," Gagne said. "This is a key opportunity for Avenor to add value for its shareholders," he said.
Gagne hinted at possible asset sales, but declined to elaborate.
Repap, which is the word Paper spelled backward, has seven large pulp and paper mills in Canada and the United States, including a big coated paper mill and two small pulp mills in Kimberly, Wis.

The buyout would end a colourful chapter in recent North American forest products history. George Petty, the gregarious and plainspoken chairman and chief executive of Repap, agreed to tender his 23 percent stake in Repap to the Avenor offer. Repap's board of directors also approved acceptance of the bid.
Petty had owned a majority of Repap, but his control of the company he founded was whittled away over the last three years as it incurred massive losses and strained under an increasing debt burden.

The debt load was the result of a C$2.5 billion ($1.85 billion) five-year capital expenditure programme that gave Repap some of the most modern assets in the coated paper business. But Petty's ambitious modernisation coincided with a long slump during the 1990s in markets for coated paper, Repap's main product.
Petty said he would join Avenor's board, but declined to comment more about his future in the merged company.
